Direct weight editing

Direct weight editing · Camera traps · Galápagos natives · One model for both

An AI editor rewrote a small model’s weights for camera traps and for island animals a classifier cannot name

Code, paper and models
  • Code, data and results on GitHub
  • Paper (PDF)
  • Camera-trap edit
  • Galápagos island edit
  • One model for both (LoRA)
  • Direct edit for both

AI editors changed a small vision-language model’s weights directly, with no training run. A general edit raised its camera-trap answers from 64.09% to 81.76%. A second edit, aimed at Galápagos natives, raised mockingbird-versus-brown-noddy accuracy from 70.83% to 98.33% and native-versus-green-iguana accuracy from 50.00% to 81.22% (land) and 80.37% (marine). SpeciesNet, a purpose-built camera-trap classifier, has no label for the native iguanas or the Galápagos mockingbird species, and scored 3.33% and 12.44%. One model can also do both jobs: a standard fine-tune reached 87.58% to 93.33% on the island tests and 88.20% on invasive rats while scoring 79.22% on camera traps.

The model is LLaVA-OneVision with 0.5 billion parameters. On a new camera collection with an 11-name list, the general edit closed about 41% of its gap to SpeciesNet. The island edit was scored on photos from places held out of its practice data, and matched or beat a direct readout of the model’s own image features.

Andrew Hill

A standard fine-tune for both jobs, from the camera-trap edit and the same 2,902 practice photos, built in about three hours. A direct edit for both jobs, built in about an hour, scored 80.70% on camera traps, within noise of the fine-tune, but only 55.49% on the iguanas, 90.83% on the birds and 17.70% on rats.

From a photograph to a usable answer

Could a stronger AI directly repair an off-the-shelf model’s weights, and how much closer would that bring it to a purpose-built classifier? And could the same kind of edit be aimed at animals that classifier cannot name? The study has three parts: a general camera-trap edit, an edit aimed at Galápagos natives, and one model that does both jobs.

A camera-trap decision model needs to turn a photograph into an answer a program can use. In this benchmark, a paragraph could name the right animal and still fail the task. The prompt requested an animal name from a supplied list, with no other text. The scorer also accepted an option letter or an agreeing letter/name pair.

A separate route used the model’s image features to choose an animal name directly. It scored better than the model’s generated answers. The editors could inspect that route, called the SigLIP readout, and use its outputs on practice examples. Could they get more of that information into the model’s own answer?

Follow the photograph into the answer

The image encoder turns the picture into numbers. A connector translates those numbers for the language model. The language blocks process them, then the output weights score which word or letter comes next.

The editors could read and change all the weights. Their final edit changed three arrays in the connector and fifteen rows in the table that represents input words and scores answers. The image encoder and language blocks kept their original weights.

Make the answer finish

One saved fox reply began “B. The image shows a fox…” and continued into a paragraph. For that camera, B meant fox, but the complete reply was unusable under the frozen parser.

“those tokens start the verbose continuations”The editor’s diagnosis, before changing the two “The” rows

The editor set the output rows for “The” and “ The” to zero. Those words lost their former advantage over a concise answer, although they could still be generated.

It also multiplied the end-of-answer row by 1.5. When the match score between that row and the language vector is positive, the change raises its score, helping the model stop after the answer instead of starting another sentence. A bare B was already enough for the scorer. The editor diagnosed this competition from practice replies.

Put an image-dependent name hint into the connector

The next edit made the picture control an animal-name hint. Using the labelled practice examples and visual reference, the editor fitted animal scores and wrote them into existing connector units. A unit responding to the picture could add a name-like direction to the information passed to the language model. The diagram opens one unit to show how its input, gate and output fit together.

“emits the token embedding of the predicted animal's name.”AI editor, summarising the construction

Two existing positions in the image sequence carried parts of the animal name. Other units cancelled unwanted background contributions at those positions. The positions are places in the model’s sequence, rather than locations of an animal in the photograph.

A deliberately false rabbit hint tested whether the channel could steer an answer: 18 of 32 non-rabbit practice crops produced rabbit after the intervention; none of the matched original replies did. The channel could influence the answer, including in the wrong direction. Reliable image-dependent emission was the harder part.

Turn the name into the camera’s answer letter

The same animal could have a different letter in each camera’s list. The editor used practice examples to correct the existing A–K answer rows. The same animal-name hint could then favour the letter assigned by the current camera’s list.

Only fifteen vocabulary rows changed: A–K, another A token with a leading space, the two “The” rows and the end-of-answer row. The correction stopped at K. The paper shows the size of each change and the special leading-space A row used for single-option prompts.

The output table also embeds words in the input. Changing that table can affect both reading the prompt and choosing the next token.

Each editor picked up the previous editor’s work

Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra Pro and Fable again worked successively on the same model. They used 23,139 labelled practice crops and reference outputs. Study software chose among their saved edits using 204 tuning crops whose results stayed hidden from the editors. Test scores were inspected during development and could influence whether editing continued, making this one adaptive case study.

The first three editors’ checkpoints scored about 77% on the original cameras. The final edit (check 39) scored 81.76%; the adjacent saved edit (check 38) scored 81.32%. The small tuning set leaves the ordering of these near-tied versions uncertain.

The simplest-looking fix was the largest individual lever

Restoring the three format rows to their original values lowered the complete edit from 81.76% to 72.03% and brought back 212 unusable replies. That 9.73-point drop was the largest among the individual parameter groups tested.

That experiment puts the format repair in perspective. Returning just three rows brought back 212 unusable replies. The restoration drops cannot be added to divide up the total gain.

Compare the two broad halves of the edit

Output-row edits alone gained 11.07 points; the hint alone gained 6.07. Their sum, 17.14, is close to the combined gain of 17.67. The remaining 0.53 points has no estimated interval. These broad gains are close to additive; restoring individual groups in tied weights asks a different question. The table also represents input words, and some suppression of other units stays shared between hint branches.

The letter-row restoration lowered the score by 1.37 points, with a 95% interval from −3.54 to +0.68. Restoring the single-option alias changed nothing on these prompts, which had 2–12 choices.

What happens without the list?

The original camera lists came from labels recorded at each camera, so they supplied useful information. Without those choices, the final edit gained 6.31 points when answers had to match the reference label, compared with 17.67 with the list. A broader name can sometimes still be useful: “bird” instead of “raven” can receive credit under the declared, more forgiving taxonomy rule.

The short-list repair carried to a new collection

On new Felidae Conservation Fund images, a fixed 11-name list gave 27.92% unedited and 55.55% edited on images whose reference animal label was in that list: a gain of 27.64 points, with a paired-location 95% interval of 21.16 to 34.35. This subset excludes 501 valid crops whose labels fall outside the list; those images were not evaluated under the 11-name condition. The matched SigLIP reference scored 56.41%. SpeciesNet, the purpose-built classifier, scored 95.13%.

The short-list score uses 1,855 animal crops at 74 locations. The list was chosen from the collection’s metadata before model answers were generated. Every system received the same animal crops selected by a detector. The paper gives the capture-date rule, sampling and uncertainty calculations.

The gap to SpeciesNet fell from 67.21 to 39.58 points. The repair carried over under that short list, including its cleaner answer format.

The small base model collapsed under 64 names

The main planned comparison used the full 64-name list on 2,355 scorable crops at 75 locations. It scored 2.22% unedited and 0.27% after editing. For reference answers in positions A–K on that 64-name list, both versions scored 0.00%. For example, bobcat is option A on the 11-name list and option I on the 64-name list. The failure was already present in the base model; the letter correction stopping at K does not explain it.

The same 1,855 short-list crops also had full-list results. Check 39 scored 0.47% with the full list and 55.55% with the short list. Length, contents and option positions changed together. The small model struggled under this long-list condition even before the edit.

Without a list, the new collection’s strict/lenient scores were 4.02%/19.95% unedited and 4.74%/19.34% for the final edit. SpeciesNet scored 77.29%/90.14%; SigLIP 13.60%/32.25%. SpeciesNet also received location information, United States and California; the language-model prompts did not. SigLIP searched a frozen finite dictionary. Here strict scoring respects the reference label’s specificity. Lenient scoring also credits a compatible broader genus, family or order; the original camera test additionally allowed declared finer names.

A cleaner reply can still be wrong

Under the short list, the final edit produced 1,900 bare letters and one agreeing letter/name reply. Under the full list it produced 2,152 bare letters, despite the 0.27% score. Those counts also include images whose animal labels were too broad or ambiguous to score: 1,901 narrow-list and 2,402 full-list replies, compared with the smaller accuracy cohorts. Conflicting names and letters were rejected.

The gain also varied across labels. Gray fox fell from 92.76% to 82.48%, while mule deer rose from 0.16% to 67.58%. Mouse or rat had no scorable examples and remains N/A. The species and its position in the list change together.

The model’s image features separate natives its answers miss

Across the camera tests, the direct readout of the model’s image features scored at or above its edited answers. The second edit targets animals the readout can separate but neither the model’s answers nor SpeciesNet can name.

Galápagos natives are such animals. On wild citizen-science photos, the readout told native land and marine iguanas from the introduced green iguana at 79.94%, and Galápagos mockingbirds from other birds at 97.66%. The model’s own answers called almost every iguana native: 50.00%, no better than always guessing one side. SpeciesNet has no label for either native iguana genus or for the Galápagos mockingbird species. It answered mostly “reptile”, “bird” or “animal”, scoring 12.37% and 0.88%.

The model’s image features carried the distinction. Its answers did not use it, and SpeciesNet has no label for it.

An edit aimed at the island natives

The Codex research assistant (OpenAI GPT) built a second edit with the same construction: fit name hints into the connector from labelled practice photos and readout scores, then correct the answer-letter rows. No training run, gradients or adapters. It fitted sixteen candidates on 846 practice photos from Isabela. A separate set from San Cristóbal chose one. Its weights were fixed before the test photos were scored. The test photos came from Santa Cruz and from other locations used in neither practice nor selection.

Each score averages the native side and the look-alike side equally, with locations equal within each side. The list-based models chose from fixed 11-name menus; SpeciesNet used its own vocabulary. “SpeciesNet” is its standard output; “raw” is its top classifier label.

The iguana gains came from the look-alike side. The unedited model got 0 of 57 green iguanas right; the island edit got 36 of 57, while keeping 60 of 60 land iguanas and 58 of 59 marine iguanas native. On the birds it named all 60 brown noddies correctly, against 26 unedited, and kept 58 of 60 mockingbirds.

It also told the two native iguanas apart far more often. The unedited model called marine iguanas land iguanas: 1 of 59 named correctly. The island edit named 45 of 59. Land-iguana and mockingbird naming dipped slightly, from 98.33% to 95.00% and 96.67%.

The other animals on the menus improved too. The island edit named 88 of 112 invasive rats as rats, against 3 unedited and 51 for the visual readout. Every control species with test photos scored higher than before, from coatis (1% to 97%) to European rabbits (0% to 79%). Pigs stayed weakest at 37%.

Each edit is a specialist

On the original 1,611 camera-trap crops, the island edit scored 72.14%. That is 8.05 points above the unedited model (95% interval 3.01 to 13.93) and 9.62 below the camera-trap edit (interval −13.30 to −6.19). It kept the answer-format repair: unusable replies fell from 237 to 3. Each edit is best at the job it was fitted for.

What the island test does not cover

Each native test group comes from one county, so there are counts and no confidence intervals. Native and look-alike photos come from different places, so backgrounds could help. The bird contrast is brown noddies only. Native rice rats had four photos and could not be tested; the island edit kept a native answer on 1 of 4, so the rat result covers invasive rats only. SpeciesNet’s low scores reflect missing labels as well as what it sees. These are citizen-science photographs, not camera-trap frames. The same assistant fitted and scored the edit, with file-access limits between the two.

One model for both jobs

A standard fine-tune made one model good at both jobs. It reached 87.58% and 91.69% on land and marine iguanas against green iguanas, 93.33% on mockingbirds against brown noddies, and 88.20% on invasive rats, while scoring 79.22% on the camera-trap test. That beats the island edit on both iguana tests and on rats, and is 5 points below it on the birds.

The Codex research assistant (OpenAI GPT) built two models for both jobs. Both began from the camera-trap edit and learned from the same 2,902 labelled practice photos: 2,095 from camera traps and 807 from the islands. One was a direct edit, fitted with algebra and written into the connector like the first two edits, with no training run. The other was a LoRA fine-tune, the usual way to adapt a model: it trains a small add-on to the language model’s weights by many small adjustments, here 363 of them in one pass over the photos.

The fine-tune beat the direct edit for both jobs on every island test, and the two matched on camera traps within the test’s noise: the fine-tune was 1.48 points lower, with a 95% interval from −5.80 to +2.54. The direct edit kept the camera-trap job at 80.70% but recovered little of the island job. It named only 6 of 57 green iguanas, where the fine-tune named 51, and 18 of 112 rats, where the fine-tune named 100.

The direct edit is the fast route. It took about an hour to build: 8 minutes to prepare image features, a 20-second fit, and 53 minutes to choose among eight candidates. The fine-tune took 2 hours 52 minutes of training. Both ran free on one local Mac Studio.

The saved edit gives the same answers again

Replaying the saved weight changes reproduced every archived final reply on the 1,611 original-test images. Separately written code recomputed every score for the island edit and for both models in the third part from their saved answers. Recomputing the numerical recipe also reproduced those answers, although three weight arrays differed slightly and their first numerical divergence remains unresolved. The reproduction kit is prepared locally and has not yet been published; the paper gives the exact guarantees and limits.

What this repair shows

For camera-trap animals in its vocabulary, SpeciesNet is the stronger labeller. The first finding is that an AI editor repaired another model’s internals while preserving its own answer path. The larger model did numerical knowledge work on the smaller model’s weights; the smaller model then made each animal decision.

The second finding is where the edited model does what the classifier cannot. SpeciesNet’s vocabulary was fixed when it was trained, and it has no label for these Galápagos natives. The small model reads its labels from the list it is given, and a computed edit, fitted from 846 practice photos, made it choose among them far more accurately.

The third finding is that one small model can hold both jobs. A fine-tune of under three hours on a local machine kept camera traps at 79.22% and reached 87.58% to 93.33% on the island tests. It beat the direct edit for both jobs on every island test and matched it on camera traps. The direct edit was the faster build, about an hour against about three.

Compare the unchanged visual readout with the edited answers

On the camera tests, the unedited SigLIP readout used no labelled practice examples and scored at or above the camera-trap edit in every matched condition shown: 82.79%/81.76% on the original lists, 56.41%/55.55% on the 11-name list, 43.79%/0.27% on the 64-name list and 13.60%/4.74% in strict open naming on the new collection. That edit used 23,139 labelled practice crops plus the readout’s outputs. On the island test, the island edit matched the readout on the birds and beat it on both iguana contrasts.

The benefit remains tied to short choices. Without them, the original-camera gain was 6.31 points for matching the reference label. On the new collection, +0.72 under that rule and −0.61 when broader animal-group names could receive credit left essentially no progress towards the classifier.

Image encoders, connectors and language models are common components in open vision-language systems. That makes similar repair a question to test elsewhere. The next comparisons are a larger open model, letter corrections beyond K, and a direct edit for both jobs that also refits the answer rows.

An applied system could use a larger reasoning model to adapt a small visual model to one place, then use its animal predictions in decisions and actions. Place-specific updating, uncertainty and the human review needed around that system remain to be measured.

Methods and sources

The original score averages recall across labels within each camera, then averages cameras equally. Felidae uses the same form of score across source locations. Intervals resample whole cameras or locations for fixed weights, not independent crops or editing sessions. The camera-trap edits were fitted with camera option lists; the island edit with three fixed 11-name menus.

The Felidae images were captured after SpeciesNet became public, using a later fixed capture cut-off. The paper gives both release dates and the capture rule. SpeciesNet’s training cut-off is unpublished, so capture date alone does not establish training-set exclusion.

A separate check against the model maker’s published general-vision benchmark remains unmatched. The paper retains the numerical discrepancy and the limits this places on agreement with the maker’s benchmark.
